fixes.explanation: I'm with you on why you'd pick it, friend. Everybody asks it. But the Teacher says not to ask why the old days were better than these, and he adds, "For it is unwise of you to ask about this." (Ecclesiastes 7:10) So he calls the question unwise.

That's right, baker. The Teacher tells us not to ask why the old days were better than these. He adds, "For it is unwise of you to ask about this." (Ecclesiastes 7:10) He doesn't say it's wise. He says it's unwise, plain and simple.

Saving up is wise advice, friend, but the verse doesn't give it as the reason. It says God made one along with the other "…so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him." (Ecclesiastes 7:14) The reason the text gives is about what a man cannot discover, not about saving.

Being humbled is a weighty thought, baker, but it's not the reason given here. The Teacher says God made one along with the other "…so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him." (Ecclesiastes 7:14) The reason the text gives is about what a man cannot discover, not about the proud.

Good guess, friend, because it sounds like something that just can't be in there. But the verse says it: "…one’s day of death is better than his day of birth." (Ecclesiastes 7:1) It's a bold line. It sits in the same verse as the good name, so the two go together.

Close, but he flips it, friend. The verse says, "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure." (Ecclesiastes 7:4) So the house of pleasure is where the heart of fools is. The heart of the wise is in the other house, the house of mourning.

You got it, baker. The Teacher says, "For like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:6) Then he adds, "This too is futile." The fool's laughter is the thing that's like those crackling thorns.

Yes, baker. The Teacher says, "Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart." (Ecclesiastes 7:7) Both warnings sit in one verse. Extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
I see the pick, friend, but the verse never mentions a king. It says, "…for anger settles in the lap of a fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:9) The word in that spot is fool.

Fair guess, baker, since a good name does show up earlier in this passage (Ecclesiastes 7:1). But in this verse the word is different. It says, "…wisdom preserves the life of its owner." (Ecclesiastes 7:12)

I can see that guess, friend, but break isn't the word. The verse says, "Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13) The thing in the question is bent, so the question asks who can straighten it. Breaking never comes up.

Not this time, baker. The verse says, "Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13) Something is bent in that question, and the question asks who can straighten it. Hiding never comes up, so only straighten fits.

That's the reason the text gives, baker. The verse says God made one along with the other "…so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him." (Ecclesiastes 7:14) Whatever comes after him, he can't discover it. That's why I keep the ovens ready and leave the schedule to God.
